section_summary: This section contains diplomatic and consular reporting on Japanese preparations for war, possible expansion toward the Philippines, military reorganization in Manchuria, anti-bandit operations, and violence by Japanese troops against Chinese civilians. It also documents Japanese fortified-zone restrictions and the recruitment of White Russian aeronautical engineers. The largest subfile is a translation of a Japanese War Office pamphlet advocating comprehensive national mobilization, military and air-force expansion, economic control, propaganda, and preparation for possible conflict with the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, and the Netherlands.

subfiles.title: Forwarding Letter for Strictly Confidential Report No. W.D. 1180
subfiles.about: Forwards Warrington Dawson’s confidential report on Japanese preparations for war.
subfiles.summary: Embassy forwards Dawson's strictly confidential Report No. W.D. 1180 on Japanese military affairs.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Preparations for War
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy in Paris and Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports French information alleging that Japan was preparing for expansion against Pacific islands, including the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: A well-connected French diplomat tells Dawson that Japan deliberately engineered its League of Nations position to enable a categorical new policy and was preparing to seize islands along the Asian coast, including the Philippines. Dawson believes the information was known at the French Foreign Office. Commander Vincent-Bréchignac separately regards war preparations as plausible, identifies the Soviet Union as Japan’s principal adversary, and stresses the need for the United States to maintain its naval program.

subfiles.title: Departmental Note on Paris Despatch No. 3421
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a Paris despatch reporting French General Staff views of Japanese activity and military capability.
subfiles.summary: Departmental note recommending a full reading of Paris Despatch No. 3421 (March 17, 1933) on Japanese military activity.

subfiles.title: French General Staff Views on Japan’s Preparations for War
subfiles.about: Reports French General Staff expectations of Japanese Pacific expansion and its assessment of Japan’s military weakness.
subfiles.summary: A French financial adviser reports the General Staff expects Japan's aggression to go beyond Jehol, perhaps to the Philippines, but doubts it can defeat a first-class power or the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Mukden Report on Japanese Military Activities
subfiles.about: Refers to a Mukden despatch from Consul Chase concerning the attitude and activities of the Japanese military.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Chase's July 19 Mukden report on Japanese military attitudes and activities in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Mukden Despatch No. 803
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of Despatch No. 803 on Japanese military attitudes and activities in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Consul Chase encloses his previous-day despatch to Peiping giving incidents and testimony on Japanese conduct in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Miscellaneous Information Relating to the Attitude and Activities of the Japanese Military
subfiles.about: Reports killings of Chinese civilians and an alleged Japanese attempt against Manchukuo commander Yu Zhishan.
subfiles.summary: Chase describes Japanese troops shooting four uninvolved Chinese farmers near Chaoyang and an apparent attempt to seize or murder Yu Zhishan, later explained implausibly as drunkenness.

subfiles.title: Conversation with a Japanese Soldier
subfiles.about: Records a Japanese conscript’s account of bandit suppression, military brutality, and conditions within the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese private educated at MIT calls Manchukuo forces unreliable and describes intimidation of civilians, machine-gunning of villagers at Hsiuyen, executions, bombing, and harsh Army discipline.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Tokyo Despatch No. 490
subfiles.about: Refers to Ambassador Grew’s despatch on reorganization of the Japanese Army in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Tokyo Despatch No. 490 on War Office plans to reorganize the Army, especially in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: The Army and the Navy
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese War Office plans for permanent Army organization and garrisons in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The War Office plans a permanent division and new garrisons in Manchukuo, using the expense to justify keeping the military budget.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Tokyo Despatch No. 611
subfiles.about: Refers to a Japanese War Department statement intended to regain agricultural support for the military.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's Despatch No. 611: a War Department effort to win farmers back to the military side.

subfiles.title: Japanese Military Motor Transport near the Soviet Border
subfiles.about: Relays a Harbin report of Japanese purchases and requisitions of vehicles for shipment toward Pogranichny.
subfiles.summary: Harbin Consul General reports the Japanese military mission bought all new trucks and commandeered hundreds of buses, moving east toward Pogranichny for an unknown reason.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch on the Anti-Bandit Drive in North Manchuria
subfiles.about: Forwards a Harbin despatch to Peiping concerning an anti-bandit operation in northern Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Hanson sends Peiping his same-day report explaining the Japanese vehicle concentration, an anti-bandit drive in North Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Anti-Bandit Drive in North Manchuria
subfiles.about: Explains that Japanese military trucks were intended for an operation in the Baoqing–Mishan–Hulin area.
subfiles.summary: Hanson reports that the trucks sent east from Harbin were assigned to a drive against brigands in the Baoqing–Mishan–Hulin area, reportedly the season’s final operation. He also describes Japanese proposals to reschedule Chinese Eastern Railway trains so that they would traverse dangerous sections near Anda during daylight.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 736, “The Military and the People of Japan”
subfiles.about: Refers to a Grew despatch discussing Japanese public opposition to military abuses of power.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 736, The Military and the People of Japan: the Diet session showed a new reaction against military abuse of authority.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Navy Department Letter on Strategic Raw Materials
subfiles.about: Refers to a report that Japan was importing large quantities of materials essential for warfare.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Navy letter on Japan's alleged acquisition of large quantities of strategic raw materials.

subfiles.title: Fortified Zones and Military Secrets
subfiles.about: Transmits a Japanese Foreign Ministry warning about violations of fortified-zone and military-secrets laws.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards a translation of a circular sent by the Japanese Foreign Ministry to diplomatic missions. The Embassy and Tokyo Consulate General planned to warn American citizens in Japan about the applicable security laws.

subfiles.title: Foreign Ministry Circular on Fortified Zones and Military Secrets
subfiles.about: Asks the Embassy to warn Americans against violating Japanese fortified-zone and military-secrets legislation.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Ministry circular on infractions of fortified-zone and military-secrets laws by foreigners; asks the Embassy to publicize the laws to Americans.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Alleged Fortifications in the Mandated Islands
subfiles.about: Refers to Grew’s report of Sir John Latham’s comments on Australian anxiety over alleged Japanese fortifications.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a May 31 despatch on an interview with the head of the Australian Eastern Mission about alleged Japanese fortification of the mandated islands.

subfiles.title: Contract of Japanese Government with White Russian Engineers
subfiles.about: Reports the passage through Port Said of White Russian engineers connected with Japanese aeronautical work.
subfiles.summary: Port Said police found White Russian engineer Margoulis carrying a letter from Japanese Naval Attaché Togari contracting him as an aerodynamic engineer in Japan; two others bound for Shanghai, possibly linked to Japanese air-force reorganization.

subfiles.title: Letter Contracting Vladimir Margoulis’s Technical Services
subfiles.about: Confirms an agreement for Margoulis to assist the Japanese Navy with aerodynamic construction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Togari confirms Margoulis will place his technical knowledge at the Japanese Navy's disposal for about six months in Japan, under a contract to follow.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 1031
subfiles.about: Summarizes the controversy caused by a Japanese War Office pamphlet on national defense and economic reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Summary of Despatch No. 1031: a pamphlet naming the U.S. and Soviet Union as enemies and urging near-socialist state direction depressed the market and heightened fears of military interference after Inukai's assassination.

subfiles.title: War Office Pamphlet
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese political and public reaction to a radical War Office pamphlet on national defense.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes a widely distributed War Office pamphlet that treats the United States and Soviet Union as possible enemies and threatens force against British or Dutch trade restrictions. Its calls for economic reorganization, agricultural relief, state-controlled media, and comprehensive defense planning alarmed politicians, ministers, financiers, and commentators as an improper military intrusion into civil affairs. War Minister Hayashi denied that the Army intended to implement the proposals, while Minobe and several newspapers criticized the publication’s militarism and radicalism.

subfiles.title: Principles of National Defense and Suggestions of How to Strengthen the Same
subfiles.doc_type: translated War Office pamphlet; partial text
subfiles.from: Section of Newspapers and News Agencies, Japanese Department of War
subfiles.about: Sets out a comprehensive doctrine for organizing Japanese society, economics, military power, and propaganda around national defense.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet defines national defense as the mobilization and control of the entire state in peace and war, rejects reliance on diplomacy or the League of Nations, and treats economic and ideological conflict as continuous warfare. It identifies the United States and Soviet Union as principal strategic rivals, demands naval autonomy and stronger Army and air forces, and contemplates force against British and Dutch economic restrictions. It advocates resource stockpiling, control of research and communications, state-directed propaganda, agricultural relief, economic reorganization, and the suppression of liberalism, individualism, and internationalism. The surviving portion ends while outlining a centralized apparatus for ideological and propaganda warfare.
